item.title: Why Rejection Hits Differently in Borderline
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

Why Rejection Hits Differently in Borderline

The role of emotional sensitivity and learned expectations in relationships.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • People with borderline may experience rejection more intensely and anticipate it more readily.
  • Expectations of rejection can shape how we interpret and respond to other people.
  • New experiences can help change longstanding beliefs about relationships.

Imagine this: You text a close friend and don't hear back. After a few hours, you might wonder whether they're busy or forgot to respond. Eventually, you put your phone down and go about your day.

For someone with borderline personality disorder (BPD), a situation like this often unfolds differently. A delayed response might bring up intense anxiety, sadness, or anger. They may become convinced their friend is upset with them, replay their last interaction looking for clues, or send several follow-up messages seeking reassurance.

What makes the experience so different?

Rejection Can Trigger Intense Emotions

People with BPD tend to experience negative emotions more frequently and intensely than others. They may also have a harder time returning to their emotional baseline after something upsetting happens. These tendencies reflect high levels of negative affectivity, a personality trait that is particularly elevated among people with BPD.

This means that an interaction that produces mild disappointment for one person might trigger overwhelming distress for someone with BPD. The emotional response is real, even when the situation doesn't necessarily warrant the interpretation of rejection.

But emotional sensitivity alone doesn't fully explain rejection sensitivity.

When You Expect Rejection, You Start Looking for It

Our expectations shape what we notice and how we interpret other people's behavior. If you repeatedly experienced rejection, criticism, or unpredictable responses from important people in your past, you may start to assume that you can’t trust anyone to show up consistently.

Let’s return to the unanswered text. Someone who generally believes that their relationships are secure will likely assume that their friend is just busy. Someone who expects rejection may immediately wonder what they've done wrong or whether the friendship is ending.

When intense emotions accompany these interpretations, they often feel like facts. The stronger the anxiety or hurt, the more convincing the belief that you’re being rejected becomes.

How Rejection Sensitivity Reinforces Itself

When you anticipate rejection, it’s natural to want to protect yourself from it. For someone with BPD, this might involve repeatedly asking for reassurance, monitoring a partner's mood, withdrawing before they can be rejected, or becoming angry when they perceive someone pulling away.

These behaviors often provide some immediate relief. Reassurance temporarily reduces anxiety. If you end a relationship before someone else does, it might lessen the sting. Anger may make someone feel less vulnerable than acknowledging how afraid they are of losing the relationship.

Unfortunately, these strategies also create problems in relationships. Repeated reassurance seeking may frustrate a partner, withdrawing obviously prevents closeness, and angry reactions may escalate an otherwise minor disagreement. When the relationship becomes strained, it can confirm the original expectation that other people will eventually reject you.

Over time, this cycle can become self-reinforcing. You expect rejection, behave in ways to protect yourself, and sometimes end up creating the very relationship difficulties you were afraid of.

Changing What You Expect From Others

One of the goals of treatment for BPD is to help people recognize that their expectations about relationships are predictions, not necessarily facts. These predictions may have developed for understandable reasons, but that doesn't mean they accurately describe every current relationship or interaction.

A useful starting point: Pay attention to your thoughts when you start to feel rejected. You may automatically accept: "My friend hasn't answered because she's mad at me." But you can try out other explanations. You might remind yourself she could be busy, distracted, or her phone may be dead.

Flexible thinking is a first step toward chipping away at longstanding expectations, but it usually also involves behaving differently in relationships so you have opportunities to collect new information.

For example, someone who typically sends several follow-up texts might experiment with sending one message and waiting. They might feel more out of control and anxious in the short term, but consider what it means when the other person eventually responds: they care enough to reach out, even when you don’t nag them.

Someone who withdraws when they feel hurt might practice telling their partner how they feel. Getting vulnerable like this can be uncomfortable, but you learn how your partner responds. If your relationship can handle a tough conversation, you get evidence that it is strong.

You’re not trying to convince yourself that rejection will never happen. Instead, you gradually learn to tolerate uncertainty in relationships, that every ambiguous interaction does not mean impending rejection, and that you can respond effectively even when someone disappoints you.

Rejection Doesn't Have to Define Your Relationships

Rejection sensitivity isn't simply being too sensitive. It reflects a combination of emotional vulnerability, expectations about other people, and learned ways of responding when relationships feel threatened.

These patterns can be longstanding, but they aren't necessarily permanent. With repeated opportunities to tolerate difficult emotions, question predictions, and respond differently, people can begin to change both what they expect from relationships and how they behave within them.

item.title: How to Get Over a Past Hurt
item.description:
Anger

How to Get Over a Past Hurt

Personal Perspective: How I learned to put the past away for a new beginning.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Understanding a bad time in the past can help you form a new beginninng.
  • The present can trigger memories of the past, but that doesn't have to be your future.
  • Reframing “I stayed too long” as “I found the strength to leave” can shift feelings of shame toward agency.
Sometimes the end offers a fresh beginning.
Source: Caroline Leavitt

Recently a best friend and I were talking about past hurts we couldn’t let go of, particularly with partners we had dated decades ago. We’re both ridiculously happy in our lives now, in our homes and careers, so why do we still bear these painful grudges — the ones that lodge like splinters and we talk and talk about with our friends? I began to wonder, what could I do to get over them? I mean, what was the point of them? I didn’t know what to do except that I was tired of giving energy to these memories. Why couldn’t I just let them go? And then, I realized that maybe I couldn’t because I was getting something out of it, and the trick was, to figure out what that something was.

Flashback to decades ago and a person we'll call Tim. I was already traumatized from the sudden death of a fiancé; I couldn’t bear the grieving and I tried everything. Despite the advice of family, friends, and therapists, I decided hurling myself into a new relationship would be the perfect salve. And I got involved with an emotional abuser. He wouldn’t let me eat. He criticized my clothing, my hair, and my friends (he didn’t want me to have any), and he controlled what I read and what activities I was forced into doing. He wasn’t affectionate. He didn’t have a sense of humor. His parents were his confidants, and I was always reminded by them that I didn’t fit into the family. I stayed because if I left, I’d grieve a man I really had loved, and Tim seemed the lesser of two evils. It was only when Tim began reading my mail without asking and, even worse, went into my computer and rewrote some of my novel, that I broke, and then I left.

The past can feel like a tangle of wires.
Source: Caroline Leavitt

I grieved again, but certainly not for Tim, whom I had no intention of ever seeing again. But my anger wouldn’t go away. Instead, it kept flaring. I thought maybe I could write about it, to get over it that way, but all that did was to freshen up the anger and remind me of the hurt and emotional violence. Maybe, I thought, what I was getting from this was expressing the anger I should have shown years ago. But who wants to feel angry forever or to be caught in a loop without any closure? Every time I had tried to talk to Tim about this, he deflected it and insisted that I was crazy, and that nowhere on earth would I find a better boyfriend. Maybe, I reasoned, I needed to have a switch in perspective.

Remember that scene in the TV show, Six Feet Under? A photographer is taking a photo of her family, and her brother says quietly, “You can’t capture this. It’s already gone.” That unlocked everything for me! I began to consider that this time that had traumatized me so much was already gone. And if it was already gone, why was I wasting time still dwelling on it and letting it affect me? That time I spent with that abusive man was a blip in time, not a continuing piece of my life.

I began to wonder what else this pull of the past might be giving me. Maybe imagining myself arguing with him, stating my case, making him see how damaging he had been, admittedly gave me a flare of pleasure. It made me feel less of a victim, and truthfully, less guilty for having been desperate enough to lead him on. So, I dug deeper until I realized something else. Maybe it was enough to know that because I had gone through that past experience with Tim, I had been changed — and for the better. Now I would never, ever let that kind of thing happen to me again. Instead of feeling shamed and angry that I stayed with a toxic beau, why not be thrilled that I finally was able to leave and cut ties and recognize a bad situation when I saw one? I had wanted Tim to rescue me from grief, but in the end, not only did that not happen, I also had to rescue myself. And in doing so, I got stronger. I stopped being a victim.

Even better, having been in a relationship that was so wrong made me know what I wanted to be right in the next one. The man who became my husband held my hand on our first date and was so silly, I was falling over with laughter, something I wasn’t used to. He was kind and didn’t criticize, and we made all our time together an adventure. And the more I was with him, the more he became my life. Remember how the conclusion of a book or movie often proclaims, "The End?” You know what? Maybe, it’s just the beginning of something healthy and new.

item.title: More Pride, Less Prejudice: Charlotte of "Pride and Prejudice"
item.description:
Identity

More Pride, Less Prejudice: Charlotte of "Pride and Prejudice"

Jane Austen created an aroace character centuries before this identity was labeled.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • "Pride and Prejudice" depicts the character Charlotte Lucas as asexual and aromantic.
  • Austen's understanding of identity is centuries ahead of its time. We've caught up with her.
The Governess by Emily Mary Osborne (1860)
Source: Google Art Project/ Wikimedia Commons

Although Jane Austen has been viewed as a writer of typical rom-coms and a chronicler of polite society, both Austen and her work have alternatively been characterized as queer. Beginning in the 1990s, a discussion known as “the Queer Austen debates” looked at Austen’s life and characters in light of various queer identities, above all homoeroticism between characters and the Austen sisters themselves.

Twentieth-century writers had laid the groundwork for queering Austen by observing that many of her characters defy gender norms and that her female characters have intense emotional relationships with other women. Even earlier, the Victorians recognized the gender-bending potential of her life and work, primarily in the theater, where the first women to play Jane and Cassandra on stage were lovers in real life and many actors “cross dressed” playing her characters. If you do a search titled “queer Jane Austen,” you’ll find additional references to essays, blogs, and scholarship as well as lists of the many queer retellings of her novels.

While the queering of Austen has revealed some crucial aspects of her work, it has been incomplete. With the exception of a handful of essays, blog posts, and internet discussions, asexual and aromantic identities have been largely ignored. But not by Austen! Charlotte Lucas of Pride and Prejudice fits the criteria for both identities: she is aroace, experiencing neither sexual desire for another nor a special warm, magnetic longing to be with someone that differs in quality even from close friendships.

Both identities are orientations, not lifestyle choices. They describe feelings rather than behavior: Asexuality is not celibacy. Neither identity is a phase and neither is pathological. Ace and aro people experience deep emotional bonds with others and the full gamut of basic emotions. They just don’t experience the feelings typically associated with intimate partnerships, which does not mean that they don’t form such partnerships. You can be ace or aro and in a domestic partnership or a marriage.

How do we know Charlotte is aroace? When she tells Elizabeth that she’s going to marry Mr. Collins, the foolish man Elizabeth herself has rejected, her friend’s tactless reaction— “Engaged to Mr. Collins! my dear Charlotte—Impossible!”—elicits a response that suggests this identity: “I see what you are feeling . . . you must be very surprised . . . But when you have had time to think it all over, I hope you will be satisfied with what I have done. I am not romantic, you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home." Which she had slim chances of obtaining: Charlotte is 27 years old, plain-looking, and lacking in family fortune, all rendering marriage unlikely. Yet marriage is the only way for her to avoid poverty, or the hardships and indignities of being a paid companion or governess, or being taken in by relatives out of pity. When Mr. Collins proposes, Charlotte readily accepts.

Elizabeth’s horror is not a response to Charlotte’s taking pragmatic factors into account in deciding to marry; such considerations were considered advisable. But marrying without any affection and for purely financial motives, although not uncommon, was not openly approved. It was considered ethical that partners should have some fondness for one another, but Charlotte admits that she accepts Mr. Collins because of what he can provide. What bothers Elizabeth is that Mr. Collins is “a conceited, pompous, narrow-minded, silly man . . . the woman who marries him, cannot have a proper way of thinking.”

Elizabeth can’t say outright that Charlotte’s behavior is immoral, but the implication of misconduct inheres in her choice of words. “Proper” means “of good character or standing . . . decent, decorous, respectable, correct.” In Elizabeth’s view, intimacy with a man Charlotte knows is foolish and whose company she does her best to minimize once married, smacks of, if not prostitution, something a bit too close for comfort. But because Charlotte is aroace, incapable of feeling romantic or sexual desire, she will be exchanging her body for an establishment no matter who she marries. The limitations of opportunity for women inevitably place her in this “transgressive” position.

Charlotte and Mr. Collins by H. M. Brock (1898)
Source: Kharbine-Tapabor/Shutterstock

Moreover, her decision isn’t as simple as she herself describes. While Charlotte knows Mr. Collins’s deficits, she also appreciates his strengths. She tells Elizabeth that “considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair, as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.”

He might be foolish, but he is an ethical man; he will respect Charlotte, and he will not be abusive or offensive, something many wives in Austen’s time couldn’t count on. His connections guarantee his success as a clergyman (his “situation in life"), enabling them to live comfortably. Later in the novel we learn that she is expecting a child; there’s a good chance motherhood will be fulfilling. Charlotte does the best with a bad lot and might indeed “have a proper way of thinking.”

Many women of the respectable classes needed to marry for financial considerations. Some had a chance at finding love, but many had to compromise, and many suffered great distress. Queer identity rendered marriage an inevitable burden, obviating even the uncertain chance for happiness accorded cis/hetero couples. And given the factors that could produce unhappiness in these “normal” couples, Charlotte is right when she claims she has as much “chance of happiness . . . as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.”

In a world that didn’t sanction queer identities, Austen once again defies norms of sex and gender, depicting a woman for whom choice of a spouse isn’t a problem, but rather marriage itself. She represents an identity that would have “dared not speak its name” if only it had a name, but which didn’t yet exist in the lexicon of queerness. Austen’s genius for understanding people manifests in her creation of a character whose sexual identity would find fuller expression and confirmation two centuries after she wrote.

item.title: The Challenges of Misophonia at the Holiday Dinner Table
item.description:
Misophonia

The Challenges of Misophonia at the Holiday Dinner Table

Misophonia can make family holidays stressful, but there are ways to accommodate.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Misophonia can add challenges to family dinners during holidays.
  • Accommodations can help families with misophonia members enjoy events.
  • Food-free traditions, quiet spaces, headphones, and breaks can help.

The dinner table is often a battleground for families where one or more members experience the misophonic response. I know this all too well as a sufferer of misophonia. Holidays are fraught with experiences that can cause sensory dysregulation, including frequent family dinners, blinking lights, loud music and events, and more. So, I ask, is the point of the festivities to spend time together regardless of the emotional aftermath, or is the purpose to spend meaningful time together?

For those who suffer from misophonia, holiday dinners can be a painful experience. Misophonia is a neurophysiological condition where otherwise normal sounds like chewing, whistling, coughing, and more cause a physiological fight-or-flight-or-freeze response. This condition was named in 2001 by Drs. Pawel and Margaret Jastreboff, and despite a growing body of research, it has not yet made it into diagnostic manuals worldwide. More recently, misophonia has been linked to neurodivergent experiences, such as sensory processing differences and autism.

The term misophonia means "hatred of sound," but hatred does not aptly describe the fight-or-flight response. Imagine you're sitting in a room, and suddenly, after hearing a sound, your heart rate skyrockets, your palms sweat, and your skin feels like pins and needles. The panic seeps in, and before you realize what you're hearing, you're feeling physical and mental distress. Unlike phobias, which often improve with gradual exposure, misophonia does not get better the more you hear; instead, the response escalates until the sufferer experiences what is often described as a shutdown, a period of intense lull, or a meltdown, a period of intense distress.

For me, misophonia often feels physically and mentally painful. If I am unable to get away from the triggering sounds, this increases. In the past, I have had to skip family events and meals because I was unable to handle the sensory distress and overwhelm. Unfortunately, there is no cure for misophonia, and the condition has a neurophysiological brain basis, as noted by Sukhbinder Kumar in his research studies. The lack of treatment can lead to more frustration on top of an already fraught experience.

Something I am commonly asked in my private practice as a therapist (LCT-C) is, "If misophonia is so distressful, how can families mitigate the distress during holiday festivities?"

The first piece of advice I always give to sufferers of misophonia, their parents, or extended family is that there may need to be adjustments to expectations over the holiday season. Families can consider activities that do not include food, such as decorating the home, going for walks to see Christmas lights if the lights are not bothersome to the sufferer, doing puzzles or watching movies without snacks, or any activity that is both social and does not lead to the fight-or-flight-or-freeze response for the individual.

Frequent breaks from family and social events can also help tolerance levels. Since sensory information is cumulative, the ability to go to a safe space and calm down is imperative. I frequently suggest noise-canceling headphones and areas where the individual can go to take breaks from the sensory stimuli. This can look like going outside, a spare bedroom at a family member's home, your own bedroom if at your home, or a bathroom if no other space is available, such as at a restaurant or public event.

The final advice I often give is that, while misophonia is difficult to live with, this does not mean that there is no hope for family relationships and events. While misophonia may make family time harder to arrange and require more accommodations, these events can still carry great meaning and importance.

Holidays can be stressful for families with or without any form of neurodivergence or necessary accommodations, but this doesn't mean that they are not worth the effort. In my own family, I have utilized regular breaks, movie nights without snacks, and the ability to come and go as needed so that I am not overstimulated. Some family members have been more understanding than others, but over time this has become the usual expectation rather than a deviation from the norm. Some families may find difficulty with extended family that does not understand sensory-based accommodations for misophonia, and in these cases I often suggest psychoeducation and tight boundaries.

Misophonia International provides free downloads for clinicians, parents, teachers, and sufferers of misophonia, including a holiday survival guide.

If there is one thing I'd like to leave individuals with misophonia, parents, or family members this holiday season, it's this: Misophonia is challenging, but there are ways to cope and accommodate the condition. A loved one does not have to understand misophonia, but they do have to respect the accommodations of the individual with misophonia.

item.title: When Getting Better in Therapy Becomes a Task
item.description:
Therapy

When Getting Better in Therapy Becomes a Task

How the stress of getting better in therapy maintains the problem.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • The more we push for change, the less acceptance a client may feel.
  • The more allowance we provide, the more stressed clients may become about not getting better quickly enough.
  • Mindfulness practice can help us develop a more neutral relationship with our own experience.

When a client treats therapy as a task and getting emotionally better as a mission, everything can become stressful.

Yet the difficulty is that different clients may need very different things. Some may need more permission, allowance, and acceptance. Others may need more practice tolerating distress without immediately retreating or giving up. And some may need both.

These needs are often interwoven.

The more we push for change, the less acceptance a client may feel. Yet the more allowance and reassurance we provide, the more stressed they may become about not getting better quickly enough.

For some clients, it can feel as though they are allowed to be only one way or the other, and that the two positions are mutually exclusive.

How the Perfectionistic Overcontroller Mode Turns Self-Improvement Into Self-Criticism

In Schema Therapy, one way of understanding this is through the Perfectionistic Overcontroller mode. This mode tries to help a client “self-improve” all the time. If they do not improve, they may criticise or punish themselves internally.

For many people, this is how they learned to show up in the world: being careful, competent, and conscientious, and always wanting to improve.

Yet this mode can also see things in very dichotomous terms: good or bad, right or wrong, success or failure. It is constantly evaluating the person internally. Sometimes it even appears during a happy moment: Am I happy enough?

We do not need to know Schema Therapy to recognise that this kind of part exists in many people, particularly those who come from competitive or demanding environments.

Why Constant Self-Improvement Can Be Difficult to Let Go of

It can be a very useful way of functioning. In some environments, it helps people thrive—or at least survive. A mindset of constant improvement may also be strongly socially reinforced. In some cultural contexts, it can earn approval, connection, attention, and even love.

This is one reason it can be very difficult to let go of.

If someone has practised this way of functioning for many years, moving away from it can feel like stepping outside their comfort zone. And sometimes the comfort zone is not comfortable at all. It is simply familiar.

At least I know how uncomfortable this is.

Outside it, I am walking into the unknown.

This can be a very tricky place in therapy. Our clients may be highly competent and may have benefited greatly from this mode being dominant in their lives.

At times, I find myself needing to stay alongside the client for quite a long time while they gradually “grow another part of themselves.” I sometimes imagine it like a tree growing a new branch. It takes time before that new branch becomes strong enough for the person to shift their balance.

Mindfulness can sometimes be a gift in this process.

Mindfulness practice can help us develop a more neutral relationship with our own experience. It gives us another place to stand. From that position, compassion and acceptance can sometimes emerge more naturally, especially with guidance.

For some clients, another difficulty is that they cannot remain with vulnerable feelings for long enough. They may move into avoidance very quickly.

And sometimes the Perfectionistic Overcontroller mode can become a camouflage for avoidance:

I am busy. I am doing something important. I am being productive.

I have repeatedly encountered another version of this over the past few years.

At times, I may be offering a form of care, presence, or limited reparenting that my client does not yet know how to receive.

I then become aware that before the intervention can really land, the client may first need to learn another way of expressing themselves—and perhaps another way of being in the therapy room.

How Relational Cultural Backgrounds Can Shape Therapeutic Needs

This has been particularly noticeable for me when working with clients from more relational cultural backgrounds.

In these contexts, interpersonal relationships may be more intense, the sense of self may overlap more with significant others, and how a person feels may be closely connected to how other people around them feel.

In these situations, a significant amount of therapeutic work may involve helping the client recognise that what is happening in the therapy room is not only an expression of “what happened.”

It may also be an attempt to manage a relational need within the therapeutic relationship itself.

The client may be communicating, protecting the relationship, trying not to burden the therapist, managing the therapist’s feelings, or attempting to remain acceptable in the eyes of another person.

In Schema Therapy terms, this becomes part of the work of strengthening the Healthy Adult mode.

The aim is not simply to help the client become less perfectionistic, less avoidant, or more emotionally expressive. It is to help them develop enough internal flexibility that striving and acceptance no longer have to be enemies.

They can want change without attacking themselves.

They can tolerate distress without immediately escaping it.

And they can receive care without needing to turn therapy itself into another task they have to perform well.

For clinicians who would like to explore these ideas in more depth, I also write about culturally responsive psychotherapy and Schema Therapy on Substack.

item.title: Is Your College Student Having a Mid-semester Meltdown?
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

Is Your College Student Having a Mid-semester Meltdown?

What parents can to do to help their struggling college student.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Validate their feelings instead of rushing to fix the problem so they feel heard and can deescalate.
  • Encourage basic daily routines for sleep, diet, and exercise to improve focus and manageability.
  • Schedule regular check-ins to monitor progress and discuss future plans to prevent rumination.

It’s October, and we’re halfway through the semester—that time of year when college students realize those bad grades actually need to get fixed since there’s just not that much time remaining. And the rest goes something like this…

Kids call parents.

Kids have a meltdown.

Parents freak out.

Parents jump in to solve the problem.

Kids ignore solutions.

Parents call me.

Look, maybe their social life is going too well, and school wasn’t a priority. They could have underlying anxiety or depression. Maybe classwork and tests crept up on them since organization and planning were something they thought they’d attend to “later.” Whatever the headwinds, here are the evidence-based strategies I recommend parents use to counterbalance the chaos.

1. Listen and Reflect

Most students don’t need advice or solutions. They need to share how badly they feel. This goes against our parental instincts to solve the problem and eradicate their pain. The problem is, this doesn’t solve the real problem. They already know what to do; they’re just struggling to do it because of some other underlying issue. This is where hard, messy lessons occur. Instead, validate how they’re feeling. Don’t agree with them; just acknowledge how hard this time is for them. Your job: Listen and then reflect. This makes them feel heard. They are more likely to de-escalate enough that they can formulate a plan out of the trench.

2. Back to Basics

Sleep, exercise, and food. If students practice consistency Sunday through Thursday with the fundamentals, intense feelings decrease, work quality increases, and their world appears more manageable. Consistency and routine don’t get papers written and test studying accomplished, but, man, it makes all of it so much easier. When I say "encourage routine," the best way to do this is by asking what their daily schedule looks like and what can be changed to make things work better. It’s also important to become part of, and role model, routine. You can do this by having regular phone calls rather than the random texts and calls we normally get. This helps struggling students think ahead and organize their day instead of making decisions based on how they feel. If they ask for suggestions (see below about offering solutions), encourage them to give every hour a home. This doesn’t mean waking up at 4:00 a.m. and doing a thousand pushups. It means being intentional about their day and week. They can schedule time for writing a paper (90 minutes is a really good chunk of time) as well as carving out time for pickleball or hanging out with friends after dinner. It’s not about going into monk-mode. It’s about planning and attending to all the important stuff we want and need to do each day and week.

3. Schedule Regular Check-Ins

If you have ever had an employer, chances are there were regular performance reviews evaluating the quality of your contributions. We need to do the same for college students whether they are struggling or crushing it. Check-ins are not punitive oversight; they are opportunities for cheerleading the ongoing successes and realigning for the challenges throughout the semester. The worst thing for a parent is the December surprise—the semester finishes, final grades are released, and your college kiddo bombed most classes. What could have been some uncomfortable but reasonable conversation is now a heated discussion about whether they can even go back for spring semester.

4. Future Focus

I really like it when parents spend time with their college students talking about stuff other than the big, hard, scary parts of current life. It’s not that I want everyone to ignore what’s not working. It’s that at a certain point, we are no longer simply sharing our struggles but getting sucked into rumination and obsessive thinking about how bad things are, how bad things will be, and how we’ll never get out. One suggestion is to plan out a few visits for the upcoming semester (you going there and them coming home). You can also get them to help figure out some details for your upcoming winter break trip. Ask for their help figuring out gift ideas for family members. Get them involved in something other than their immediate life at school. Get their brain focused on something other than the current challenges, if only for a few minutes each call.

5. Solutions…as a Last Resort

Learning from friction is essential, but that doesn’t mean we should let them crash head-on into a wall. There comes a point where most students have legitimately tried changing things their way and realized it’s not working. When they ask for help, and I mean really ask for help, that’s when it’s appropriate to offer guidance. How can you tell what’s rhetorical and what's not? The rhetorical questions are actually masked statements like "How can I possibly manage all the stupid assignments for this course? The professor is never available during office hours, and there's nobody around to assist me." What they’re really saying is that they’re either not interested or feel unmotivated to do the work. A legit question is framed very differently, like “I'm considering dropping this class. What options do I have, and what steps should I take?”

Summary

The halfway point of the semester is no-man's-land. We’re too far from the starting line to quit and too far from the finish line to feel any relief. With structured guidance, strategic support, and the ability to process difficult thoughts and feelings, your student can successfully move through these challenges and maybe even gain meaningful skills that extend far beyond their academic credits.

item.title: The Black-Boxing of Reality
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Black-Boxing of Reality

What happens when AI allows us to build a world we can no longer understand?

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • AI's internal computations can exceed our ability to explain them.
  • AI discoveries may become difficult to translate into human understanding.
  • We may build a world whose workings increasingly escape our comprehension.
Source: Tommy Diner / Unsplash

Let's start with a question. What happens when our ability to discover new things moves beyond our ability to understand them?

But first, let's take a step back. I think it's fair to say that science has typically had a bit of distance between discovery and explanation. We find something interesting, and then we try to figure out why. And there's an expectation that understanding will eventually catch up. It's almost like "knowledge causality" where the two are linked.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may be complicating or even breaking this linkage in ways we have not fully considered. I think there are two different problems we need to address. The first concerns the extraordinary computational capabilities of AI. The second is a little stranger and, to me, much more interesting. It's our ability to understand what all that computation actually means, particularly in the context of human cognitive capabilities.

The Limits of Computation

The complexity of AI is often hidden behind the simplicity of the user experience. Large language models (LLMs) operate in an almost "ethereal complexity" of numbers and dimensions. The math behind these systems is well understood, but the enormous number of interacting relationships makes it difficult to explain precisely, well, what the heck is actually going on.

This is the ongoing problem of AI interpretability. We know the way that AI is constructed, and we're even making progress in understanding its inner workings. But the sheer complexity of their computations may exceed what any human could reasonably follow.

There's something important here. Just because we can't follow every calculation doesn't mean we can't understand the result. We use computers to solve problems that would take us lifetimes to crunch the numbers ourselves. The answer, however, arrives in familiar terms that we can work with.

So far, so good. But there's another boundary ahead—one that may be much more difficult to cross.

The Limits of Understanding

What if an answer becomes incomprehensible to humans?

Imagine AI discovering relationships across thousands of interactions. The relationships may be mathematically valid and extraordinarily useful. But the discovery itself might exist in a form that doesn't really translate into anything a human can understand or conceptualize.

Sidebar: It might be fun to get a sense of this complexity with a few back-of-the-envelope calculations. GPT-3, an older model, contained 175 billion parameters and operated across 12,288 dimensions. Meta's Llama 3.1 expanded that to 405 billion parameters and 16,384 dimensions. Don't try to understand this explicitly; just try to get a sense of the profound complexity of today's LLMs.

So, we can describe the math. But making sense of what all those relationships actually represent is another matter entirely. We might be able to test the result and establish that it works. Or maybe another AI could even use that discovery to develop something new. But across this sea of complexity, humans could remain unable to understand the "first-principle" relationships that give the answer its meaning and utility.

A Strange New World

Humans have always used mathematics to explore things we cannot visualize. Complexity alone doesn't make something unknowable. But AI establishes the strange possibility that some discoveries may remain beyond our ability to have a meaningful explanation. And that holds true even when we can demonstrate their usefulness.

So, here's the key insight: AI intelligence may allow the advancement of knowledge to become independent of human understanding.

Think about that. One AI makes a discovery that humans cannot adequately explain. And then another AI builds upon it, even building on relationships that remain outside our comprehension. A third develops something new from those earlier discoveries. The process continues, and knowledge advances without necessarily passing through the human mind in any meaningful or interpretative way.

The Black Boxing of Reality

Simply put, the black box is a system we can use without really understanding the inner workings—we know what goes in, we observe what comes out. But imagine that construct moving beyond the computer itself. AI-generated discoveries become the foundations for new discoveries, which become the foundations for still more discoveries.

We could eventually inhabit a world whose underlying structure and organization are built upon discoveries that we can't fully translate into our understanding. AI might work exceptionally well. We could test them, use them, and even improve them. Yet important parts of their output might remain intellectually inaccessible to us.

There's a psychological consequence here that I find fascinating and critical. We like to understand things, particularly the things that shape our lives. Understanding allows us to question an answer, challenge an assumption, and frolic in the world of discovery. The physicist and Nobel laureate Richard Feynman captures this perfectly in the title of one of his books: The Pleasure of Finding Things Out.

Push on this a little bit, and here's what we might get. We get progress that no longer requires understanding. We become comfortable accepting results simply because they work. And our confidence could become detached from understanding. And when that happens, our curiosity may begin to change as well. It's a precarious spiral predicated on the simple idea of "Why bother?" Why bother to understand something when the next (AI) discovery is already waiting?

I think it's important to recognize that this isn't a pessimistic view of AI. AI may ultimately help us explain things we never could have understood on our own. But there's another possibility that deserves some reflection. We may become extraordinarily capable of creating things while becoming less capable of understanding what we've created. And that may be humanity's greatest paradox.

Science has helped cast a light on the mysteries of our world. Now we may be developing intelligence that allows us to create mysteries of our own—building upon them and into the fabric of everyday life.

The black box may eventually become the world itself.

item.title: Masculinity and Accountability in the Duke Football Incident
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Masculinity and Accountability in the Duke Football Incident

Lessons in emotional regulation, responsibility, and role-modeling.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Positive masculinity involves self-control as well as loyalty and action.
  • Emotions can explain behaviour without excusing it.
  • Public accountability can model emotional maturity for young athletes.

A brief sideline interaction during a recent Duke University football game has generated a deeply divided public response. After a Duke player went down injured, athletic trainers rushed onto the field to provide medical assistance. In the moments that followed, Duke defensive back Kimari Robinson appeared to swat away a female athletic trainer who was attempting to create space around the injured player. Robinson later issued a public apology, explaining that he was concerned for his teammate and acknowledging that his reaction was wrong.

Since then, debate has exploded across social media. Some viewers see a young athlete reacting emotionally in a stressful situation and believe the incident was overblown, while others claim that it was an unacceptable act of aggression toward a medical professional carrying out her role during an emergency. What’s striking from a psychological perspective is not simply the incident itself, but how differently people interpret it. Thousands of people can watch the same footage and arrive at entirely different conclusions about what happened, who was at fault, and whether an apology was necessary at all.

Positive Masculinity Means More Than Taking Action

One reason for this divide may be that the incident touches on competing ideas about masculinity. For many boys and young men, masculinity is associated with action. A good man steps in. He protects his friends. He takes charge when something goes wrong. In sport, these expectations are often reinforced by cultures that prize toughness, loyalty, and standing up for teammates (Vierra et al., 2023). Viewed through this lens, some observers interpreted Robinson's actions primarily as those of a concerned teammate reacting emotionally to seeing a friend injured. Yet positive masculinity isn’t always about acting. Sometimes, it’s about knowing when not to act.

In high-pressure situations, strength is often demonstrated through self-control rather than intervention. Zhang et al. (2024) found that athletes with stronger self-control are better able to make effective decisions under pressure and are less likely to allow emotional reactions to dictate their behaviour. Although stressful situations can still influence their judgment, self-control helps to determine whether those emotions ultimately shape the athlete’s behaviour. This reflects an important psychological distinction between understanding someone’s behaviour and excusing it. We can acknowledge fear, anxiety, anger, or distress without concluding that such emotions automatically remove personal responsibility for our actions.

Why the Apology Became Part of the Story

One of the most revealing aspects of the Duke situation has been the reaction to Robinson's apology. While some welcomed it as an acknowledgment that a mistake had been made, others argued that he should not have apologised at all. Comments suggesting that the matter should have been handled privately, or that an apology was unnecessary, became almost as prominent as discussion of the original incident. From a psychological perspective, this raises an important question. Why do public apologies provoke such strong reactions?

Part of the answer may lie in how people understand accountability. Some may view accountability as being synonymous with punishment, blame, or public humiliation. Viewed through this lens, an apology can be perceived as evidence that someone has been pressured into admitting wrongdoing. But of course, accountability doesn’t necessarily mean condemnation. At its most basic level, accountability involves recognising that our actions affect other people and accepting responsibility when our own behaviour falls short. Nobody’s expected to be perfect, but when we get something wrong, it's important to take responsibility for it.

One of the clearest signs of maturity is the ability to acknowledge wrongdoing without becoming defensive or seeking to minimise its impact. Understanding why something happened is important, and can help us learn from mistakes. Conversely, the reasons behind the behaviour, however compelling they may be, shouldn’t turn an apology into a justification for the actions or dilute responsibility for the harm caused.

What Do We Want Young Athletes to Learn?

Athletes occupy highly visible positions in society. Whether they want the responsibility or not, they are role models. In fact, Kelly et al. (2024) found that athletes were among the most influential role models for young people, with male adolescents particularly likely to identify high-profile athletes as role models. This means that young men watch how these athletes respond to adversity, conflict, correction, and stress and use that to model their own behaviour. They learn not only from moments of success but also from how their favourite athletes react when things aren’t going well. How do the athletes conduct themselves when stressed or upset? How do they respond when they make a mistake? Seeing athletes take genuine accountability for their actions and reflect on what they can do better going forward teaches the young men watching that making a mistake does not diminish strength. If anything, it shows confidence, self-awareness, and emotional maturity.

Ultimately, the most interesting question raised by the Duke incident is not whether a young athlete made a mistake during an emotionally charged moment. Most of us can agree that mistakes happen. The more important question is what we can learn from moments like these. Like the fact that strong emotions shouldn’t be used to excuse behaviour that would otherwise be unacceptable or that genuine strength includes self-control, accountability, and respect for those trying to help.

item.title: Rewriting Your Menopause Story
item.description:
Menopause

Rewriting Your Menopause Story

Small lifestyle changes can make a big difference during menopause.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Regular movement can help protect bone health and support overall well-being.
  • Adjusting your diet and daily habits may help ease common menopause symptoms.
  • Mental stimulation and stress management can support cognitive and emotional health.

Menopause may not be fun, but it doesn’t have to be a time of decline, either. More than one-third of women’s lives will be lived in a post-menopausal state, and new studies are finding that we have more control over our menopause story than most of us thought. In fact, we can actually improve our health and well-being during and after menopause. The secret to success is thinking of menopause as an early alert system and learning how to take action.

Improving Health and Well-Being in Menopause

  1. Increasing your physical activity during perimenopause and menopause can help to counteract bone loss and even improve your bone integrity. The good news from the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN) is that even a little exercise and activity can go a long way.1 You don’t have to join a gym or build an entire new fitness routine. If you’re not already active, try walking at a moderate pace for 1 hour, three times a week.2 Walk in the mall, backyard, or even the office; take the stairs more often if you can; or just close the door to your bedroom, turn on music, and dance for 10 minutes. Any rhythmic activity is less fatiguing than static stances since you are alternating muscles. It is also more soothing because it’s repetitive, and we know exactly what is coming next. That’s why we rocked babies, and now we’re rocking ourselves.
  2. Decreasing your sugar intake can decrease your belly fat, your cravings, and your fatigue. Did you know that all three of these menopause symptoms can be related to hormonal changes, and not just aging? This was a new learning for me. Apparently, as estrogen drops during menopause, insulin resistance increases, and that means glucose stays in our bloodstream longer and triggers weight gain around the waist.3 Then, when the increase in circulating glucose is followed by a sudden drop, the drop triggers carbohydrate hunger and sleepiness. I have all three: waist weight gain, candy cravings, and fatigue after meals. Decreasing my sugar intake has not been easy, but I’m seeing results, and I'm relieved that these are three symptoms that are not inevitable signs of aging.
  3. Learning to limit caffeine, alcohol, spicy foods, and stress may be among the most important changes we can make for our postmenopausal health. These adjustments can also help us manage daytime hot flashes and nighttime sweats that disrupt our sleep. We all know we should try to avoid stress, but many of my patients tell me that it took hot flashes to actually motivate them to learn deep breathing, take yoga classes, join a therapy group, or practice mindfulness exercises.
  4. Keeping your brain active is especially important during menopause. If you spend a lot of time looking for your keys or phone and trying to remember names, you’re not alone. The good news is that even though brain fog complaints are common during menopause, they are not usually signs of dementia.4 They are generally signs of menopausal hormone fluctuations disrupting brain activity, increasing fight-or-flight cortisol levels, and disrupting sleep from hot flashes. They are usually temporary and improve post-menopause when hormone fluctuations quiet down.5 Think of brain fog as a call to brain action—keep using it. A 44-year longitudinal study reported by the American Academy of Neurology found greater mental activity in midlife was associated with a lower risk of dementia and a 46 percent lower risk of Alzheimer's disease later in life.6 So, keep doing those crossword puzzles, don’t watch the news before bedtime, use reminders and calendars, and find opportunities to laugh, because laughter increases our brain’s serotonin output and serotonin is a neurotransmitter involved in social memory and word-finding.

Although we can take more control of our health and happiness, if menopause symptoms are disrupting your daily life, please enlist your physician’s help and find emotional support. Your doctor can help stabilize your hormones, and your support group or counselor can help stabilize your emotions. You don’t have to rewrite your menopause story on your own.

item.title: 10 Truths Teens Want You to Know
item.description:
Adolescence

10 Truths Teens Want You to Know

What I’ve learnt as a psychotherapist working with adolescents.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Adolescence is a period of development but it's not "just" a phase.
  • A key developmental task of adolescence is individuation, and it's not linear.
  • Physical and psychological separation is another adolescent task and they need parents' help.

As a psychotherapist, I’m gifted a front-row seat to the wonderful world of adolescence. It really is a privilege to hear about their experiences and be invited into their internal worlds as they share their thoughts, feelings, fears, and fantasies. Everyone I’ve met over the three decades I’ve been supporting teenagers and young adults is unique, of course, and what we talk about is confidential, obviously, but there are some things I’d like parents and carers of teens to know, and that the teens would like you to know, too.

1. It’s not “just” a phase

Young people are frequently told that whatever they’re going through is “just a phase,” the implication being that they’ll grow out of it, get over it, or change their minds about whatever “it” may be. Preceding anything with the prefix “just” is minimising and disrespectful. You’re not “just” a mum. They’re not “just” a kid. And it’s not “just” a phase. Adolescence is a period of development, sure, but it’s a significant life stage, and those who are growing through it deserve that acknowledgment.

2. Uncertainty doesn’t mean disingenuousness

The fluidity of young people’s thought processes is frequently displayed as ambiguity, confusion, and uncertainty. One minute they’re into something—like really into it—and the next they’re over it. Their ambiguity illustrates the fluidity of adolescence per se and relates to the fluidity of gender and sexual identity in particular. Ambiguity and confusion are ordinary developmental processes, as young people contemplate who they are and wonder about their place in the world. Be patient while they work it out.

3. You don’t know everything—and you don’t need to

Parents don’t know everything about what their children are up to. Even the ones who think they do. Even the ones who check their children’s phones. Secretly checking your children’s phone demonstrates you are not to be trusted, and they really need to be able to trust you, so please don’t. If you want to know what they are up to, ask them. But know this: They won’t tell you everything, and they’ll tell you even less if they think you’ll judge them, lecture them, confiscate their phone or minimise their experiences.

4. Don’t confiscate their phone

Previous generations of teenagers watched TV, read magazines, listened to bands, stuck posters of the ones they fancied on their walls, spoke to their friends about sex—who was doing it, how, and who wasn’t. Contemporary teenagers are doing the same, except they don’t have to be shackled to a landline or invest in physical music players or magazines that tell them how to French kiss or issue posters of celebrity crushes. All this stuff is in their phone. Don’t take it away.

5. Online life is real life

People meet, hang out, and communicate differently in the modern world—through social media, online gaming, and dating apps. Meeting on a dating app is not inferior to meeting offline. An online friend is not less of a friend than the ones at school. If you dismiss your child’s online friends and relationships as “not real,” the conversation’s over; they won’t talk to you because you’ve demonstrated you don’t get it. If you really don’t get it, ask them to help you understand.

6. Development is nonlinear

A key developmental task of adolescence is individuation—the process of becoming a fully formed person with an identity and a robust enough sense of self. The process isn’t linear; it’s experimental. That’s why they keep changing their minds. Bear with them.

7. You need to let them go

A related task is physical and psychological separation, and you’ve been preparing your teens for that since day one. You helped them to manage separations between feeds, then during the school day, then through free time and sleepovers. The task of separation will go better if you’re both on board. If you’re not willing to let them go, they’ll pull harder.

8. It’s all big

Teenagers’ lives often seem theatrical and chaotic—both internally and externally. Big stuff is happening—even if it doesn’t seem big to you—and they have big feelings in response. Validate those feelings, don’t negate them—and please don’t pathologise them.

9. Stay tuned

Adolescence is like a “must-see” drama playing out in real time. Sometimes it’s a psychological thriller, or a romance; other times they’ll throw in a comedic twist. You have a never-ending subscription to the wonderful, turbulent world of adolescence. Stay tuned (in) and stay curious.

10. Listen and love them

Even when it feels like they are pushing you away, what teens need most of all is to be listened to and loved.

My books You’re Not My F*cking Mother and Other Things Gen Z Say in Therapy (PCCS Books, 2024) and Stop F*cking Nodding and Other Things 16-Year-Olds Say in Therapy (PCCS Books, 2022) are collections of fictional short stories about the lives of teenagers and young adults.

item.title: How to Know if Your Partner Is 'Micro-Cheating'
item.description:
Micro-Cheating

How to Know if Your Partner Is 'Micro-Cheating'

Micro-cheating isn't as trivial as its name makes it sound.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Micro-cheating involves partner behaviors that make you question their emotional or physical commitment.
  • Having trust in a partner is crucial in predicting whether a relationship will remain free of turmoil.
  • People who had cheated in a previous relationship are more likely to cheat again in a subsequent relationship.
Source: SHVETS production / Pexels

In an ever-changing world, we’re becoming more open to nontraditional relationship formulas—be it open relationships, live-apart marriages, or even lifelong singlehood.

We are probably also seeing a rise in “micro-cheating.”

Micro-cheating involves actions or behaviors by your partner that make you question their emotional or physical commitment to your relationship. These can include actions like regularly texting someone they find attractive or obsessively liking their social media posts.

Since these behaviors are not blatant instances of cheating, it can be tricky to confront or deal with a partner who may be micro-cheating. This can lead to a slow erosion of trust, which can spell disaster for a relationship.

Trusting your romantic partner is integral to a fulfilling and happy relationship. In fact, science tells us that having trust in a partner is crucial in predicting whether a relationship will remain free of troubles and turmoil.

A 2020 study published in Psychological Reports found that a lack of trust in your partner can wreak havoc on your relationship, leading to emotional instability, conflicts, and even the intention to break up. What’s more, people who don’t trust their partner are more likely to snoop through their cell phones, which can make the problems worse.

Here’s a major warning sign that your partner may be micro-cheating and what you can do about it.

You Keep Uncovering ‘Harmless Secrets’ About Your Partner’s Friendships

If you found out that your partner (with whom you share a monogamous relationship) slept with someone else a couple of months ago, you would naturally feel betrayed. It’s a simple case of cause and effect.

On the other hand, if you found out from your partner that they have been having lunch with an attractive coworker for a few weeks now, you may find yourself in a more ambiguous spot when it comes to processing the information.

You might be inclined to do one of two things, neither of which is ideal:

  1. You might confront your partner about why this was kept a secret from you. In this case, your partner may feel you are accusing them of cheating or that you are insecure about your relationship with them. This can quickly go from a sensitive situation to one that could irreversibly degrade the trust you have built over time.
  2. You might ignore it as a piece of information that is not relevant to your relationship. In this case, you are giving your partner the benefit of the doubt and assuming they just forgot to mention it to you because it wasn’t important to them. However, it could also cause you to ruminate about what else they may have forgotten to mention.

What You Can Do About Newly Uncovered Secrets

Rather than jump the gun on the issue, emotionally separate yourself from the information you just received. Weigh the signs that your relationship is strong, happy, and fulfilling against the signs that your partner has one foot out the door.

For instance, before you react to the secret that was kept from you, ask yourself the following questions:

  • How meaningful is this information to you?
  • Has your partner ever given you a reason to doubt their faithfulness?
  • Have you kept similar secrets from your partner? What was your motivation behind keeping this information secret from them?

Once you take a moment to collect your thoughts and assess the situation, explain to your partner that you were blindsided by the information they have just given you. As you broach the topic, it is important to maintain a tone of curiosity, not accusation. Allow your partner to respond while keeping an open mind.

Remember, micro-cheating is more subjective than physical infidelity. Your partner most likely didn’t think much of their behavior, but that doesn’t mean that you have to sweep it under the rug.

As hard as it may be to hear, if your partner has a history of cheating, even the most innocuous behaviors that fit the description of micro-cheating should be viewed as a red flag. A 2018 study published in the journal Archives of Sexual Behavior found that people who had cheated in a previous relationship were three times more likely to cheat again in a subsequent relationship.

This suggests that past infidelity is a strong predictor of future infidelity, and that some people may have a tendency to engage in repeated acts of dishonesty or betrayal. Therefore, if you notice that your partner is frequently texting, flirting, or hiding things from you, and they have cheated before, you may want to reconsider whether you can trust them.

That said, all relationships are unique, and each one is a work in progress. Some flirting outside the relationship is natural, according to Giulia Zoppolat, a psychologist and lead author of a 2022 study about the romantic attraction we feel toward people who aren’t our partners:

“It is normal to have attractive alternatives in one's life; this is not necessarily a threat to your relationship. What makes people pause and re-evaluate things is when there are strong feelings of desire towards someone else, which is a stressful situation. I would argue that it is important to recognize this stress and acknowledge that mixed and conflicting feelings are normal in this situation. This does not mean that the relationship is necessarily doomed, just that it might require a bit more attention to sort out one's feelings and decide what the best course of action is, whatever that may be.”

Understanding and addressing behaviors that border on infidelity require acknowledging that there is not a one-size-fits-all solution. The "right" resolution is unique to you and your partner. If you sense secrets being kept that cause feelings of betrayal, engage in an open dialogue with your partner. Clear communication rooted in empathy and understanding is the cornerstone of long-term relationship satisfaction.

item.title: The Anatomy of Estrangement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

The Anatomy of Estrangement

10 common patterns that can drive parents and their adult children apart.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Parents may inadvertently create the very distance from their adult child that they fear and worry about.
  • Parent and child estrangement rarely has a single cause and usually develops from overlapping patterns.
  • Preventing, understanding, and resolving estrangement requires parental self-reflection and accountability.
Source: geralt / Pixabay

In the previous post, we were discussing the beginnings of estrangement between parent and adult child, and how the empty-nest stage is often characterized by rips and tears in the fabric of the family.

I have observed many common pathways that painfully (and sometimes irreversibly) point families in the direction of estrangement during this phase.

Here are some typical ones:

  1. Chronic criticism, control, and conditional acceptance: Adult children may distance themselves from parents who persistently judge their choices, undermine their autonomy, or communicate that parental approval depends on achievement, obedience, or conformity.
  2. Emotional neglect or lack of emotional attunement: A parent may have provided well from a material standpoint and fulfilled many responsibilities while remaining emotionally unavailable. Adult children may describe feeling unseen, misunderstood, or mischaracterized while they were growing up.
  3. Abuse, intimidation, or persistent emotional insecurity: Histories of physical, sexual, or psychological abuse; coercion; threats; or frightening parental anger may lead adult children to limit contact to protect their safety and well-being, even though they are aware that they are no longer as vulnerable as they were when they were younger.
  4. Unresolved childhood conflicts and injuries, along with failed attempts at acknowledgment: Estrangement may follow repeated and futile efforts by an adult child to discuss painful experiences while growing up, particularly when the parent responds to these efforts with denial, minimization, defensiveness, or counteraccusation.
  5. Boundary violations and difficulties accepting young adult autonomy: Some parents continue to intrude into their adult children's decisions about academic matters, careers, partners, finances, parenting, or personal lives. Distance may become a way to establish boundaries that are not being honored and respected.
  6. Divorce, remarriage, and divided family loyalties: High-conflict separations, disparagement of one parent by another, perceived abandonment, unequal treatment, and tensions involving stepparents and step-siblings can lay the groundwork for relational ruptures.
  7. Rejection of identity, values, or intimate relationships: Estrangement may develop when parents explicitly reject an adult child's sexual orientation, gender identity, religious beliefs, political views, choice of partner, career decision, or other important aspects of identity. The fundamental source of pain is often the experience that love and acceptance are conditional.
  8. Addiction, untreated psychiatric difficulties, or chronically destabilizing behavior: Substance misuse or abuse, unpredictable behavior, repeated crises and emergencies, or harmful conduct associated with psychological difficulties can undermine trust and lead adult children to protect themselves through distance.
  9. Conflicts involving spouses, partners, grandchildren, or extended family: Disagreements over access to grandchildren, perceived favoritism amongst siblings, loyalty expectations, and competing family obligations may intensify existing tensions. Sometimes the apparent dispute is the final expression of much older relational difficulties.
  10. Accumulated disappointments and incompatible accounts of family history: Not all estrangements follow a dramatic event. Some emerge from years of missed opportunities for connection, repeated misunderstandings, and incompatible narratives regarding what family relationships have meant. As I often muse to myself during difficult family therapy consultations, there are families who seem to never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity for contact, communication, and reconciliation.

Of course, these pathways are rarely discrete and neatly differentiated, and frequently overlap. For example, an adult child's decision to limit contact with their parent can be the result of a combination of factors, including years of perceived criticism (#1) and emotional neglect (#2), issues that were never allowed to be discussed with their parent (#4), who may still feel ashamed by several years of alcoholic behavior (#8) as their child was heading into adolescence.

In the family that I wrote about in the previous post, #1 (Robert’s parental approval of Andrew depends on Andrew’s continued conformity to his religious upbringing), #5 (Robert is not respecting Andrew’s differentiation), and #7 (Robert cannot tolerate what he perceives as Andrew’s rejection of his dearly held religious values) seemed to be at work.

So when Robert came to meet with me to discuss his concerns about the growing distance between him and his son, and asked me to help “bring him back to the fold,” my initial focus was on illuminating for him the ways in which he, as a father, was inadvertently creating the very reality that he was trying to avoid by sitting in judgment of Andrew and refusing to express interest in Andrew’s independent journey.

In my next post, we’ll take a look at how the process unfolded.

item.title: Wonder-Centered Education Begins With Educators
item.description:
Education

Wonder-Centered Education Begins With Educators

Fostering wonder in educators may lead to richer student inquiry.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Wonder-infused learning can engage students in inquiry, experimentation, and “joyful struggle.”
  • Teachers who share their own wonder can help students feel more comfortable expressing uncertainty.
  • Educational leaders can cultivate wonder through professional development and school culture.

In the past few weeks, three people involved in education have brought wonder in the classroom back to my attention. Angela Stockman is reconsidering her work in educational assessment and facilitation after reading the book Tracking Wonder. She wrote in her Substack recently,

"How might tracking wonder, rather than curiosity, offer richer rewards? How might it make it my documentation practice more meaningful? I’m not sure. But… a practice that slows us down enough to stay open, that gives our curiosity something real to work on, that treats bewilderment as a legitimate place to stand, that produces the evidence hope requires, that puts us in the company of colleagues, and that gives us a way to admire one another out loud and deepen the qualities we admire in our own selves? That seems like a profoundly rewarding practice that might help me find surprising answers.

I think this is where documentation can begin to widen the aperture around what it means to be a teacher or a professional learning facilitator."

Another person is seeking a Doctorate of Education (EdD) and is directly involved with a university center that provides educators with professional development. Her EdD focus? Wonder. A third serves on a board of education and a teaching and learning committee as educators and school leaders in her state reconsider their priorities and how they assess learning. Their questions have me wondering about education itself and about educators.

Consider this post a timely update from "The Creative State of the Union: 6 Bold, Wonder-Centered Ideas for Obama’s Education Initiative," which I wrote in response to fellow wonder-tracker and psychologist Todd Kashdan’s post from 2011, "3 Ideas to Prevent Schools from Killing Creativity, Curiosity, and Critical Thinking."

My questions now: What would happen if we placed wonder closer to the center of education? and What would happen if we began with the educators themselves?

It’s possible. I’ve witnessed the most seemingly jaded educators and educational leaders reignite their capacity for wonder. And that capacity can be contagious.

What Happens When Students Wonder?

But let's start with students and educational design. With deliberate design, educators and educational leaders can foster a necessary ecosystem of wonderers.

A March 2026 phenomenological study showed—in my subjective view—stunning and encouraging results. Led by Andrew Gilbert and Steph N. Dean of Clemson University, the researchers studied an eight-week “wonder-infused” project with students in grades 3-5. Although science-directed and situated in an outdoor learning laboratory, the project gave students considerable freedom to pursue what fascinated them. Teachers set up outdoor stations across related fields of study. Students kept wonder journals, recorded observations and questions, pursued self-selected scientific phenomena, and participated in a culminating Wonder Fair.

Students discovered wonder as an adventure with immediate relevance to their lives. As one student described it, “Well, it kind of helps you open up your mind… it helps get you ready for the world. It helps you figure out answers on your own.” With the teachers' guidance, students learned to move from their initial wonderings toward testable questions and their own experiments. Wonder for its own sake seemed to become a meaningful part of the learning experience.

The researchers also found evidence of what they call "joyful struggle." The students struggled in coming up with hypotheses and then getting collaborating students to agree. But the joyful context of wonder made the struggles more light-hearted. Every adult I work with, frankly, would savor a culture of “joyful struggle” because struggle is inevitable in meaningful work.

Wonder spreads, and in and of itself seems like a relevant “outcome.”

But What About the Teachers?

I want to back up. In the Clemson study, teachers themselves participated in the wondering and what researchers identified as “shared vulnerability.” Teachers shared their wonders with students, encouraging students to share theirs. One teacher noticed how often she'd walked through the woods without really seeing anything. Dean particularly is on a mission to help science teachers regard themselves as part scientist and part educator. So, this approach is to get teachers to regard themselves as scientists in wonder themselves, as scientist-educators who do not always have the answers but who often share questions with their students.

In their work on “wonder-full education,” Wolbert and Schinkel suggest that teachers' own capacity to wonder is essential to cultivating wonder in students. They note that such teachers do not simply view wonder as some mechanical element to deliver a lesson, but they more or less inhabit contemplative wonder (to wonder at) and inquisitive wonder (to wonder about—and more in line with curiosity in the Tracking Wonder Framework).

Their research also points toward vulnerability. They note that wonder can expose our vulnerability because it reminds us of how much we don't know. Teachers, accustomed to being expected to have answers, must sometimes be willing to admit their uncertainty. In my observations, that openness can create conditions in which students feel free to wonder themselves. Teacher and students are questing and wondering together.

Other research points in a similar direction. Gilbert and Byers' 2017 qualitative study of preservice elementary teachers out of George Mason University found that wonder-based pedagogy helped participants reconsider their relationship with science and envision new possibilities for teaching.

And I want to call out something else. Too often, wonder-centered pedagogy focuses on elementary school children. I've been saying at least since 2010 that “Wonder is not kids' stuff. Wonder is radical grown-up stuff.”

For years, I've worked with adults to help them recognize and cultivate different facets of wonder. In workshops with undergraduates at Western Connecticut State University and doctoral students at Boston College, for instance, I have seen how much permission adults sometimes crave to wonder openly. There is often a palpable relief in recognizing that they can practice wonder and integrate it into their academic and professional lives.

How many educators have opportunities to rediscover what first excited them about learning? And what happens to their students when they do?

Cultivating a Culture of Wonder

Wolbert and Schinkel describe the need for a schoolwide ethos of wonder. Such an ethos is not unlike the work I have done with leaders and teams of adults.

So, here are three invitations to consider and share with educators and leaders you care about:

  1. Let questions live longer. Teachers don't have to turn every question immediately toward an answer or measurable outcome. Students and teachers alike can make some room for uncertainty and inquiry, for receptive wonder. Rather than jumping to answer questions, teachers can have students record more open-ended questions or questions that students could research. Teachers also can practice humility and say, “I don’t know. Let’s explore that together.”

  2. Give educators experiences of wonder themselves. Professional development usually emphasizes skills, standards, techniques, and outcomes. What would change if some educator development also restored teachers' own curiosity, imagination, and sense of possibility? What if a faculty meeting or professional development day included time for educators to explore a question that genuinely fascinates them? What if they were invited to notice what has become overly familiar in their classrooms? What if they were trained in practices, project design, and classroom culture that engender wonder? A teacher's own wonder could become a starting point for professional learning.

  3. Build cultures where wondering is encouraged. Fostering wonder cannot depend entirely on an inspired teacher or one elaborate project. For educational leaders, where do their assessment systems, meeting agendas, and professional expectations encourage exploration? Where can teachers admit uncertainty, experiment with an approach, elicit delight, or bring an unresolved question to colleagues?

Maybe bringing wonder back to education begins before the lesson plan. Maybe it begins with the adults who design the learning environment. What are they still in wonder with? What has surprised them lately? Where are they allowed to experiment?

So much is possible.
