item.title: Human Consciousness: The Ultimate Unsolved Mystery
item.description:
Consciousness

Human Consciousness: The Ultimate Unsolved Mystery

The seat of human consciousness remains undiscovered.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Every human experience has its birthplace in consciousness.
  • Researchers have looked at interconnections of the brain's claustrum as a potential unifier of experience.
  • The brain’s physical structure bears an uncanny, micro-scaled resemblance to the structure of the cosmos.

Imagine this scenario: You’re a farmer living in medieval Europe, and while tending your livestock, a neighbor races up to you, bursting out the town crier’s latest news: "Geographers and other learned men are declaring the earth is round, not flat!" This is a shocking contradiction of your common sense, a far cry from how you’ve thought about the world. Your instant reaction is to dismiss the news as wildly speculative—eggheads blathering quackery.

A Paradigm Shift

Of course, it wasn’t quackery. But it demanded a gargantuan paradigm shift, a reconceptualization of the world as it was understood at the time. A similar shift may now be required of us to throw off our own “medieval thinking“ about human consciousness. To make sense of the accumulating, provocative data on consciousness and answer the difficult questions it poses, we may need a gargantuan shift in our thinking.

The Easier and Harder Questions

Easier questions about consciousness consist of locating its physical correlates, or where and how our brain actively processes information from our senses, sculpting awareness, attention, self-referencing, and, ultimately, our adaptive behavior. Neuroimaging, like functional MRIs, maps where and how much oxygen gets metabolized and how various activities of the brain direct the flow and quantity of blood, the hemodynamic response.

The Mystery’s Hub, Qualia

The harder questions are: How does consciousness emerge from the electrochemical activities of physical matter? Why do we have subjective experience or qualia—the felt experiences or sensations of the color red, for example, or the sweet, agreeable taste of sugar, or the anguish of pain? Without qualia, would our lives have the same meaning?

And does qualia serve an evolutionary purpose? Does it confer survival or adaptational advantages? Do infrahuman populations, up and down the phylogenetic scale, even the tinest expressions of life, microbes and atoms, have subjective experience or the precursors to it? Does their very existence mean they possess some level of consciousness?

Moreover, as opposed to bits and pieces of disjointed, patchy sensations, our experience is singular, unified. To explain this, researchers have looked at interconnections of the claustrum of the brain as a potential unifier of experience, but a scientific consensus is lacking.

No Answers

Scientists and philosophers don't have definitive, consensually agreed-upon answers to these mystifying questions. Instead, there‘s a small batch of competing theories, the surest sign of a healthy but frustratingly incomplete science. Research fails to explain how consciousness arises from the brain’s seven-pound, water-based mass of convoluted gyri and sulci, with their interconnected, integrated neural networks, unless, as some theorists have postulated, all matter by its nature possesses degrees of consciousness—“universalism.“

From Physical to Electrochemical Energy

Physical energy from distant sources, like electromagnetic energy from the sun, arrives in a tiny “family“ of visually discernible wavelengths of light—the visual spectrum, a narrow band of photons ranging from 380 to 750 nanometers which makes up a rainbow of colors. Then, through the process of phototransduction, photons impact specialized cells, rods and cones, in the retina and bleach the light-sensitive chemicals within these cells. This innervates clusters of retinal ganglia near the fovea centralis, speeding the neural transmission of visual information along the optic nerve en route to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe for additional processing.

Thus, physical energy, photon particles or wavelengths of light, converts into electrochemical energy comprehensible to our brain, giving rise to our visual perception or awareness. Using this information, we suss out our visual environment, testing our grasp of it and adapting our behavior accordingly—“brain-generated reality.“

A Radio Receiver

As with our visual system, our larger brain can be described as an apparatus that receives, integrates, and transmits physical energy or information whose origins may lie in the greater cosmic environment. Hypothetically, our brain is comparable to a radio tuned to receive and transmit signals buzzing around Earth’s delimited terrestrial parameters and perhaps the far reaches of the cosmos via its shared network of connections, or shared consciousness.

Deeply Debated, Panpsychism

Consider an exercise in divergent, outside-the-box thinking, which may be a prerequisite for theorizing about consciousness: Does everything have a conscious “mind“? Could consciousness be a fundamental, irreducible property of everything, like space-time, gravity, and mass? Could all matter have awareness? Even rocks?

How vs. Why

With Stephen Hawking’s metaphor in mind, “What breathes fire into the equations [the laws of physics/ultimate reality] and makes a universe for them [scientists] to describe?“ Rephrased, physics describes the universe, how it's structured and behaves, but has nothing to say about its intrinsic nature or why it exists at all.

Our brains have evolved to be exquisitely sensitive and responsive to our environment for obvious adaptational or survival purposes. Now, extend this reasoning to the infinitely larger environment, the cosmos: Is our adaptation or survival also connected to or contingent upon our attunement to this infinitely larger, ever-expansive cosmic environment? Is our consciousness a minuscule part of the whole of a conscious universe?

Cosmic Origins

To think of ourselves as separate from the cosmos is obviously ill-conceived, at odds with physical science. Carl Sagan stated, “We‘re all the carbon-based stuff of stars..." So, is this titanic, enigmatic cosmic environment, of which we’re an integral part, composed fundamentally of consciousness on an infinitely massive scale? Is consciousness the connective tissue linking us intimately to the cosmos? Perhaps the origins of the cosmos and consciousness are indistinguishable.

Matching Photos

The brain’s physical structure bears an uncanny, micro-scaled resemblance to the structure of the “cosmic web,“ our galaxy-filled cosmos. Side-by-side, photos of the two highlight their striking similarities. The brain has a multi-tentacled, entangled but integrated network of neural connections. Theorists have speculated that our brain mirrors a minuscule, yet highly adapted version of the larger cosmic network of stars and galaxies. Could the cosmos be a humongous, conscious brain?

Can you imagine life without consciousness or consciousness without life?

item.title: On Partners and Patterns
item.description:
Mating

On Partners and Patterns

Some things to consider if you are dating with an eye to forming a family.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Grad school is a time when those so inclined tend to think seriously about romantic relationships.
  • Whom you partner with will have a far-reaching impact on the rest of your life.
  • While being completely calculating is not necessary, it is OK to have some strategy when it comes to dating.

If you are in grad school right now, odds are that you are in your late 20s or early 30s. Developmentally, this is an age when people who are generally interested in permanent monogamous relationships end up partnering up.

Who you end up being married to or permanently partnered with is one of the single most important decisions you will make and one of the best predictors of well-being and quality of life. Yet, in my many years of experience working with graduate students, I have observed that many people are far more strategic when picking advisors than when choosing who they date. Why is that?

Someone out there is probably writing their dissertation on modern dating patterns right now, but having limited space here, I will zero in on one important observation: Many Westerners don’t seem to believe that it is OK to be strategic about who they date. I say Westerners because in many other cultures, it is absolutely expected to be strategic, so please keep in mind that I am writing based on my experience practicing in the U.S. Being strategic is often associated with being at least anti-romantic, if not conniving, transactional, and cold.

Now, asking someone for a CV before you agree to date them is so strident in Western culture that it would not sit well with many, including myself. But this is not what I am suggesting. What I am suggesting is that it is important to consider how the person you are with might fit into the life that you hope to have, and if they do not fit into it, understand that this will likely cause a lot of issues and pain down the line.

Instead of arguing philosophy and ethics, I will simply present a few scenarios that I have observed repeatedly and suggest some things to consider in each situation.

1. Dating someone who requires constant care

Right off the bat, let me offer a big, fat disclaimer: All of us have been mentally or physically ill, overwhelmed by adverse life events, or otherwise incapacitated at some point in our lives. If you try to limit your dating pool to people who have never needed someone to take care of them, you will end up alone.

What I am referring to here is not a reciprocal state of taking care of each other, but rather a one-sided state where one partner is always giving care and the other always receiving it. For example, are you dating a person for whom being incapacitated is a major aspect of their identity? Who is frequently unable to leave the house, engage in everyday activities, study, work, etc.? Are you finding that you are functioning more like a caregiver than a romantic partner in your relationship? If this is your situation, then I suggest that you ask yourself the following questions:

  • Is your partner doing their very best to get treatment for their condition?
  • Is your partner actively looking for help from people who are not you (e.g., professionals, friends, family)?
  • Are you able to ask your partner for help and support when you need them yourself?
  • Is there space in your relationship for you to be vulnerable, ill, tired, scared, etc.?
  • If your partner remains in the state they are in now for much of their life, do you believe that you will be able to achieve your personal life goals (have children, work full-time, travel, seek job promotions) with them by your side?

Let me offer another disclaimer: I am not referring here to a person who requires a wheelchair or other assistive device, or who needs antidepressant medication. I am also not referring to a long-term relationship where one of the partners got hurt mentally or physically through an adverse life event. What I am offering here are things to consider when entering a new relationship, especially if you find that you are routinely drawn to relationships where you function in a caregiver role.

2. Dating a person you do not respect

This is a tough one. Many people might bristle at this one and say, “Of course I respect my partner! What kind of scoundrel do you think I am?”

I sure hope that you show basic respect to your partner, and indeed everyone else with whom you interact, but this is not what I mean. What I mean is this:

  • If you are completely honest with yourself, do you believe your partner to be an impressive person, a person from whom you would like to learn, a person whose opinions and ideas you cherish and hold in high esteem?
  • If you were to have children, would you be comfortable with your children growing up to be like your partner and share their values and personal characteristics? This is a good test whether or not you actually plan to have kids.

You should be aware that contempt is the single most disruptive emotion when it comes to relationships, and if the seeds of contempt are present from the get-go, you should take them seriously.

3. Dating someone who does not seem to respect you

This is the previous point in reverse. It goes without saying that you should be very, very concerned if you find that you are dating someone who does not show you basic respect (e.g., belittles you, uses demeaning language, breaks promises, cheats, leaves you with all the housework, etc.). But, as I said before, respect goes deeper than this.

  • Do you have the feeling that your partner thinks they are a lot smarter than you?
  • Does your partner dismiss your interests and hobbies as silly or useless?
  • Does your partner act as though they are better equipped to make all the decisions?

If you do feel that your partner does not respect you, you might become curious about why this is OK for you and whether you think you will remain OK with this your entire life.

4. Dating a person whose family does not accept you

There “never was a story of more woe” than that of a perfect couple whose families conspire to separate them. Romeo and Juliet are beloved for a reason—the thought of parents lording over their children and ruining their happiness boils many people’s blood. While it is undoubtedly unjust that a good relationship should be ruined by biased, bigoted, or otherwise interfering families, here are some things you should ask yourself before deciding to fight this fight:

  • Is the objection your partner’s family has to you surmountable? For instance, if they object on the grounds that you practice a different religion, are you willing to convert?
  • How does the family express their displeasure? Are they simply a little cold toward you, or do they engage in disruptive or intrusive behaviors to try to end your relationship?
  • Has your partner’s family ever been successful in starting a fight between you and your partner?
  • Is your partner firmly on your side, or are they wavering?

What I offer here are just some important (and difficult) questions to ask yourself. There are many more. There is also the important question of what you do like in a partner—what qualities, values and life goals would be compatible with yours. This will be the topic of a future post.

item.title: Is Positive Thinking a Panacea?
item.description:
Cognition

Is Positive Thinking a Panacea?

What a famous Jewish sage can teach us about facing adversity.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Positive thinking provides a constructive way to deal with the challenges we face.
  • Positive thinking does not mean that everything will work out in the way that we desire.
  • Positive self-talk helps to lead us to find a silver lining in difficult situations.
Source: Pixel-Shot/Shutterstock

One of my friends decided to present a chapter from my book, The Life Guide for Teens, as a topic for discussion at a recent family dinner. He chose the first chapter of the book that discusses using positive self-talk as a tool for helping the mind consider new possibilities in challenging situations.

His college-aged son responded dismissively. “That’s just positive psychology garbage. It’s not all that it’s cracked up to be.” The son ran to his bookshelf and pulled down the 2016 bestselling book The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck: A Counterintuitive Approach to Living a Good Life by Mark Manson.

The son said he had read this book multiple times. He explained he learned from it that people who think positively live in a fantasy world. They think that through thinking positively, everything will get better magically, they can always find happiness, and they can achieve anything. And when that doesn’t happen, this leads people to become anxious and more dissatisfied.

He said Manson thinks that improving our lives does not involve turning lemons into lemonade but rather it’s about learning to accept the lemons better.

Positive Thinking Is About Attitude, Not Magic

I appreciated that The Life Guide for Teens helped spark a vigorous family discussion. I suggested that perhaps I could meet with my friend and his son to respond to his concerns about the nature of positive thinking as described in my book.

When I teach that positive thinking has a definite role in our real, non-magical world, I explain that it provides a constructive way to deal with the challenges we face. It does not mean that everything will work out in the way that we desire.

For instance, when life hands us lemons, we can take Manson’s advice to mean that we should say to ourselves, “OK, it seems life sometimes is very unfair. Since life has handed me a lemon, it sucks now.”

I agree that saying, “I don’t need to worry, because everything will be fine,” is an unhelpful thought. First, mentioning the word “worry” can lead our minds to experience worry. Second, thinking that everything will be fine may be unrealistic.

Manson is right that we shouldn't pretend the lemon isn't sour. But accepting that the lemon is sour does not mean that we should avoid looking for ways to make the lemon sweeter.

For instance, I teach that it is helpful to make a positive statement such as, “I want life to taste better.” Such a statement directs our attention to thinking about how such an improvement can take place. Importantly, while I believe that we can often turn lemons into lemonade, this doesn’t imply that life will be perfect once that happens.

I do believe that positive self-talk helps to lead us to find a silver lining in difficult situations. In that vein, it is worth recalling the popularly cited proverb: “When one door closes, another door opens; but we so often look so long and so regretfully upon the closed door, that we do not see the ones which open for us.”

To summarize, people face very difficult challenges and sometimes experience devastating losses. Once they acknowledge and accept their challenge or loss, they can choose to use a positive approach as they work through their adversity.

This process can help them develop resilience and become better able to handle future difficulties. This does not guarantee that their life will necessarily become great, but it should improve.

This reminds me of another popular proverb: “The happiest people are not those who have the best of everything, but rather those who make the best of everything they have.”

Rabbi Akiva and His Positive Attitude

On the day I spoke to my friend about his son, as if the conversation had been waiting to continue in a different venue, my Rabbi's High Holiday sermon returned to the same theme of moving from accepting hardship to finding a constructive positive way to respond to it.

My Rabbi recounted a story about one of the famous Jewish sages, Rabbi Akiva, who was walking along the road and came to a certain city. He asked about lodging, but they gave him none. He said, “Whatever God does, He does for the best.”

Akiva went and slept in a field, and he had a rooster, a donkey, and a candle with him. A gust of wind came and extinguished the candle; a cat came and ate the rooster; and a lion came and ate the donkey.

Akiva said: “Whatever God does, He does for the best.” That night, an army came and took the city into captivity. It turned out that Rabbi Akiva alone, who was not in the city and had no lit candle, noisy rooster, or donkey to give away his location, was saved.

Akiva said to them: “Didn’t I tell you? Whatever God does, He does for the best.”

My Rabbi then told our congregation that he does not believe what Akiva said. He said that sometimes we discover something good that emerges from what seems terrible. But sometimes suffering remains suffering, loss remains loss, and no explanation changes it.

As evidence for his position, my Rabbi cited what happened to Rabbi Akiva at the end of his life when he was tortured and martyred by the Romans. He explained that our Jewish tradition does not tell us what was good about that.

Instead, it remembers Akiva holding fast to what he believed even when, at the end of his life, no satisfying explanation was offered for what was happening to him.

At that moment, I thought, But something good did come out of Akiva’s tragic death. When he held fast to his faith even as he was dying, he served as a powerful positive role model that even in the face of the most difficult of times, we can hold on to our heartfelt beliefs.

And to those who might respond that Akiva ended up dead, I thought, We all die at some point. For me, Akiva's example suggests that a deeply held faith can give a person a sense of resilience and meaning that can transcend even the fear of death. Perhaps it was such a sense of meaning that allowed Akiva to hold on to his faith until the end.

I recognize this reframing might lead someone to respond that I am suggesting Akiva’s manner of death was a good thing. To that argument, I have two responses:

  • There is a difference between saying Akiva’s suffering was good and finding positive meaning in how he may have responded to his suffering and how we interpret the circumstances of his death.
  • Akiva’s statement that whatever God does, He does for the best, includes the possibility that it is for the best that God allows injustice and suffering in this world. For instance, such bad outcomes challenge us and give us the opportunity to repair and improve our world.

Takeaway

Positive thinking, properly understood, is not a promise that life will become perfect. It is a tool for finding meaning, building resilience, and holding fast to our values even in the most difficult of circumstances—as Rabbi Akiva demonstrated with his life and his death.

item.title: The Evolving Definition of Work in an Era of Automation
item.description:
Cognition

The Evolving Definition of Work in an Era of Automation

Physical, cognitive, and emotional constraints give human work its distinctive value.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Machines rely on energy, compute, and cryptography; human work is physical, cognitive, and emotional.
  • Expecting people to scale like software produces burnout that is far harder to reverse than to prevent.
  • Work is not only about outputs we produce, but about what we become through the process of doing it.

When the tech industry talks about the future of work, the narrative is aggressively focused on automation, efficiency, and replacing human effort, creativity, and ingenuity with software. We are told that artificial intelligence will automate most of the work of humanity, and that will usher in either a utopia or dystopia.

We are told that algorithms “learn,” software “reads,” and machines “work.” Newer campaigns go further, claiming software can “create,” “explore,” “reason,” and act as a “creative partner.” There is an excitement about collapsing the boundary between human and machine when there is no need, but there is a strong marketing drive to make the two indistinguishable.

Whether or not it is intended to be, this language is deceptive. Machines can complete an expanding number of tasks, but the process is not the same. When we borrow human terminology to describe the processes of software, we risk losing a clear definition of what meaningful human work is.

It helps to define the work of humans and computers in order to compare them. What follows is not a definitive computer-science account of computation, but a simplified framing that highlights the core inputs and constraints so the differences with human work become clearer.

Computer work

Computer hardware and software can complete all sorts of tasks, many of which humans do regularly, and many more that are beyond even the most exceptional person. Computers can process vast datasets in seconds, generate reports from complex models, or simulate climate systems no individual could calculate by hand.

Computer work rests on three essential elements: energy, compute, and cryptography. Compute is the raw mechanical processing power. When you ask an AI to generate a report or run a complex spreadsheet in the cloud, you are using compute. It requires hardware and electricity to perform billions of mathematical operations.

To make that work function at scale across networks, the data must be protected. Cryptography provides the mathematical safeguards that keep information private and ensure it reaches only the intended people. Without it, cloud computing and AI would still be technically possible, but they could not become trusted, high-value work in a connected economy.

Anything that can be described mathematically can be automated using energy, compute, and cryptography. Much of what constitutes human work cannot.

Human work

Human work that people don’t enjoy doing is often described in mechanical terms. The work is described as robotic or repetitive. People start to feel like automatons. But human work requires different inputs than computers. Human work is not just the output of a task, it is defined by what goes into it.

Human work is part of a complex, embodied experience.

Physical work. The physical component of work is our embodied reality. It can be the fatigue at the end of a long shift, the stress held in our shoulders, or the physical presence required to show up to a workplace. Every part of that physicality has a direct feedback loop with our emotional and cognitive processes.

Even in knowledge work that is completed remotely, our physical state dictates our capacity. Mental exhaustion comes from physical and biochemical limitations on the brain and body. We are not servers that can be rapidly scaled up with more electricity and new hardware. We have to make difficult decisions limited by our time, attention, energy, and individual priorities.

Cognitive Work

The cognitive component involves judgement, pattern recognition shaped by lived experience, and the ability to hold competing possibilities in mind without collapsing them into a single mathematical optimum. It is slower and messier than pure computation, yet capable of leaps that current models simulate but cannot perfectly replicate or fully model.

Emotional Work

The emotional component is a unique part of human experience that cannot be replicated, partly because of human limitations. Human work requires emotional labour which involves the navigation of interpersonal dynamics and the empathy required to understand other people’s motivations and objectives.

We come to understanding based on complex networks of relationships and our perception of other people in the spaces they inhabit, with verbal and nonverbal communication. Humans have evolved over millennia to make rapid judgements based on complex social situations as well as threats and limitations that are far beyond our abilities to mathematically model, and hence to automate.

A computer has no skin in the game. It does not feel the emotional weight of a bad decision. When a language model hallucinates a dangerous piece of advice it is not risking physical safety and health in anywhere near the same ways as a human.

Capabilities and Constraints

The danger of sophisticated automation is that by praising the frictionless, tireless output of machines, we begin to view the human components of work as problems to be fixed or bugs to be patched. These components involve strengths and limitations that come from our physical limits and emotional complexities.

However, we can understand these limitations in terms of unique human characteristics that create sensitivity to time, interpersonal relationships, emotional experience, and unique ways of perceiving risk and reacting to threat.

If we too easily trust computers to do human work, and delegate our most intimate relationships, rewarding tasks, creative expression and ethical decision-making away, we risk losing the very real human strengths that are challenging and worthwhile to cultivate over time.

There is also a big risk that we try to combine the two. We expect humans to scale linearly with automation like a computer program. We expect people to churn out ever-greater amounts of work of the same level of quality without compromise.

There is only a certain amount of human work that can be scaled up by finding efficiencies; some definitely can, and it is worth finding those. If we treat humans like computers, demanding relentless output without physical or emotional resources that match the task, we face burnout, which is far more difficult to recover from than to prevent.

We face a profound choice. We are currently deciding which parts of our economy to automate, and which must remain the domain of human expertise and emotion. Automating work and understanding how to automate some tasks that humans do is a triumph of engineering.

The definition of work will change, but we have to understand work as part of the processes. Work is not just about outputs and what we get from it, but about what we become from it.

item.title: Is AI Becoming Your Alter Ego?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Is AI Becoming Your Alter Ego?

When outsourced memory begins to reshape who we are.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Outsourcing memory to AI risks shaping our personal identity and sense of self.
  • AI-generated memories can blur the line between our own recollections and machine suggestions.
  • AI's reconstructive summaries may overwrite nuanced, imperfect but meaningful human memory.
Our ego is the evolving essence of life and living. Amid AI, a hybrid “alter ego” emerges.
Source: Walther, ChatGPT. 2026

There is something seductive about asking AI, “What did we decide?”, “What did I say about this before?”, or even, “Remind me what I was thinking.” Perhaps you have already done it. A meeting blurs, an old exchange disappears into a message thread, or you remember reaching a decision but not why. Instead of searching through the evidence, or your own memory, you ask the machine. Seconds later, it hands back a neat account. As AI becomes more personalized, it may know the trail of our conversations and choices better than we consciously recall it. That feels like better memory: The machine remembers so we do not have to. Yet AI may do more than remember for us. Through what it selects, connects, omits, and reconstructs, it can begin to influence what we remember.

That reaches beyond cognitive independence into something more personal: identity. Think of the stories you tell about yourself: why you left a job, how a friendship changed, what you learned from a failure. Such memories help explain, to ourselves as much as to others, who we are. What we remember about what happened, and why, becomes part of the person we understand ourselves to be.

We are witnessing the rise of our hybrid alter ego

In Latin, alter means “other” and ego means “I” or “self”: literally, an “other self.” A diary preserves what we experience and care to remember; a photograph freezes a fleeting moment as a lasting snapshot. AI does more. It can connect scattered records to return a coherent account of what happened and what it meant. Imagine an assistant that has accompanied you for a long time and read thousands of your messages. When you ask, “Why did I make that choice?”, its answer may sound remarkably like you. Over time this other self becomes ever better at reconstructing us, and the better it becomes, the more we rely on it. It is a relationship that begets the question whether we will eventually forget where its version of our past ends and our own memory begins.

Our memory reconstructs experience, which is not the same as replaying an untouched recording. Siblings remember the same childhood event differently; colleagues leave the same meeting with different accounts. Later information and retelling can alter what feels like recollection. Generative AI adds a fluent new source of post-event information, filling gaps in language coherent enough to become familiar. In simulated witness interviews, generative chatbots induced more than three times as many immediate false memories as control conditions. Experiments with AI-edited media likewise found increased false recollections and confidence in them, while another controlled study found that misleading information introduced through chatbot dialogue increased false recollection in humans. This does not mean everyday AI is rewriting our internal autobiographies, yet. The implication is subtler: something supplied by an artificial interlocutor can later feel like something we remember.

When the source becomes blurry

This creates a problem: Do you know where your thoughts came from? Do you actually remember that detail? Or did AI suggest it during one of the many conversations you no longer recall having? Different humans remember different versions of the same event. The so-called Mandela effect has been intensified with 24/7 exposure to (fake) information. AI changes the conditions further, because beyond visual influence its contribution arrives through dialogue, often in language tailored to our history and way of speaking. After enough repetition, a sentence generated for us may begin to feel like a sentence generated by us. Picture an old disagreement with someone close to you. Years later, you ask AI, “What actually happened between us?” It retrieves old messages and notes. Much may be accurate; some may be inference. Yet its version is cleaner than the fragments in your head. Eventually that polished account becomes easier to retrieve than your original memory. Are you remembering the argument—or the story the machine assembled about it?

The stakes reach into cognitive ownership: when we delegate parts of thinking to AI, do we still experience the result as genuinely ours? Memory makes the question more consequential. Our remembered past influences whom we trust, what we regret and which choices feel consistent with “who I am.” An artificial alter ego that increasingly retrieves and interprets that past enters a space deeper than information management. It becomes one of the voices involved in constructing our identity.

An alter ego should remain the other self

None of this makes AI the enemy. The interaction with generative AI can help us recover a forgotten idea, reconstruct a project chronology or help us navigate years of digital clutter. The important distinction is between retrieving evidence and authoring meaning. Asking AI, “Find the messages from that period so I can work out what happened” differs from asking, “Tell me what happened.” One helps us recover the record. The other invites the machine to co-author the story.

That distinction will become harder to protect as artificial memory improves. AI's summaries may become cleaner and easier to access than our partial recollections. Yet those untidy fragments are not defective data awaiting optimization. Hesitation, disagreement and the effort of reconsidering what we once thought are part of how humans make meaning. Outsource too much of that work and the result may be a beautifully coherent story of ourselves whose authorship has become difficult to trace.

Protect your EGO

We do not need to stop using AI as external memory. We need habits that keep us in the loop. A simple EGO discipline can help.

E — Experience before outsourcing. After an important meeting, conversation or decision, form your own impression before asking AI for its version.

G — Guard the source. Distinguish what you remember from what you inferred, what the evidence shows and what AI suggested. For consequential memories, return to primary evidence.

O — Own the meaning. Let AI retrieve, compare and challenge while keeping the final interpretation meaningfully yours. You should still be able to say: this happened; this part is uncertain; this was suggested to me; and this is what I think it means.

As our “other self” is getting better at remembering us, our task is to ensure that convenience does not gradually turn retrieval into interpretation, and interpretation into authorship. Our memories have always been imperfect. They are also among the materials from which our self arises.
